paragraphs: Tom Cruise is one of the most famous celebrities in the world. However, his new film, Digger, is turning into an enormous failure. For such a big star, the start was unexpected. It opened to only $8 million at the domestic box office over the weekend of October 2. The domestic box office means theaters in the United States and Canada. Reportedly, the film could lose about $245 million, according to the magazine Variety.

In its second weekend, ticket sales fell by 60%. That is a remarkable drop. After two weekends, the film had earned $35.3 million around the world. Variety now expects it to finish with about $50 million in total. That is far below what it needs, and the gap is remarkable.

Why is the loss so enormous? Making a film is expensive, and selling it is expensive too. Warner Bros. reportedly spent around $100 million on a global marketing campaign. Moreover, theaters keep roughly half of the money from ticket sales. So a film must earn much more than its costs before the studio makes any money.

Variety says Digger needs about $350 million worldwide to break even, or to earn back its costs. A person speaking for Warner Bros. disputes that number and says the point is closer to $300 million. The precise number is not clear. Reports also dispute how much the film cost to make, so the precise cost is not clear either. Still, every estimate is far above $50 million.

Critics were divided. The film started with a score of 52% on Rotten Tomatoes, a website that collects reviews. Viewers on the first night gave it a weak grade. Warner Bros. even put good and bad reviews side by side in one ad and asked viewers to "decide for yourself." Furthermore, Hollywood celebrities such as Anne Hathaway and Jane Fonda publicly praised the film on social media.

Their praise did not change the numbers. Fortune compares Digger with other famous failures, such as John Carter and The Lone Ranger. Each of those films reportedly lost around $200 million. Compared with them, the loss for Digger could be larger by a considerable amount.

The timing is also hard for Warner Bros. On October 6, Paramount Skydance closed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, the studio's parent company, for roughly $110 billion. Just a year ago, the 103-year-old studio had big hits. In 2026, however, it has had several expensive, disappointing films. For its new owner, the acquisition now has an unexpected start: a failure that everyone can see, happening very publicly.
